newMicroscopyPlates.title: Connective Tissue Proper
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: Fibroblasts produce this fibrous tissue. Connective tissue proper includes the fixed cells fibrocytes, adipocytes, and mesenchymal cells. LM × 400. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Adipose Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: This is a loose connective tissue that consists of fat cells with little extracellular matrix. It stores fat for energy and provides insulation. LM × 800. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Reticular Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: This is a loose connective tissue made up of a network of reticular fibers that provides a supportive framework for soft organs. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Diagram of Spongy Bone
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: Spongy bone is composed of trabeculae that contain the osteocytes. Red marrow fills the spaces in some bones.
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Blood: A Fluid Connective Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: Blood is a fluid connective tissue containing erythrocytes and various types of leukocytes that circulate in a liquid extracellular matrix. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Pseudostratified Ciliated Columnar Epithelium
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Seromucous glands provide lubricating mucus. LM × 680. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Four Types of Tissue: Body
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: The four types of tissues are exemplified in nervous tissue, stratified squamous epithelial tissue, cardiac muscle tissue, and connective tissue. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Types of Cartilage
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: Cartilage is a connective tissue consisting of collagenous fibers embedded in a firm matrix of chondroitin sulfates. (a) Hyaline cartilage provides support with some flexibility. The example is from dog tissue. (b) Fibrocartilage provides some compressibility and can absorb pressure. (c) Elastic cartilage provides firm but elastic support. From top, LM × 300, LM × 1200, LM × 1016. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: The Three Types of Muscle Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: The body contains three types of muscle tissue: (a) skeletal muscle, (b) smooth muscle, and (c) cardiac muscle. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Muscle Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: (a) Skeletal muscle cells have prominent striation and nuclei on their periphery. (b) Smooth muscle cells have a single nucleus and no visible striations. (c) Cardiac muscle cells appear striated and have a single nucleus. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Nervous Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: Nervous tissue is made up of neurons and neuroglia. The cells of nervous tissue are specialized to transmit and receive impulses. LM × 872. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Dense Connective Tissue
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: (a) Dense regular connective tissue consists of collagenous fibers packed into parallel bundles. (b) Dense irregular connective tissue consists of collagenous fibers interwoven into a mesh-like network. From top, LM × 1000, LM × 200. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Structures of the Respiratory Zone
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: (a) The alveolus is responsible for gas exchange. (b) A micrograph shows the alveolar structures within lung tissue. LM × 178. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Histology of the large Intestine
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: (a) The histologies of the large intestine and small intestine (not shown) are adapted for the digestive functions of each organ. (b) This micrograph shows the colon’s simple columnar epithelium and goblet cells. LM x 464. (credit b: Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Epidermis
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: The epidermis is epithelium composed of multiple layers of cells. The basal layer consists of cuboidal cells, whereas the outer layers are squamous, keratinized cells, so the whole epithelium is often described as being keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. LM × 40. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

newMicroscopyPlates.title: Juxtaglomerular Apparatus and Glomerulus
newMicroscopyPlates.caption: (a) The JGA allows specialized cells to monitor the composition of the fluid in the DCT and adjust the glomerular filtration rate. (b) This micrograph shows the glomerulus and surrounding structures. LM × 1540. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
newMicroscopyPlates.license: OpenStax CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; retain the specific micrograph credits in the caption

notIncluded: No proprietary Complete Anatomy assets, unlicensed videos, generated patient anatomy, or a complete female model.

organReferencePlates.title: Internal Structures of the Heart
organReferencePlates.caption: This anterior view of the heart shows the four chambers, the major vessels and their early branches, as well as the valves. The presence of the pulmonary trunk and aorta covers the interatrial septum, and the atrioventricular septum is cut away to show the atrioventricular valves.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Gross Anatomy of the Lungs
organReferencePlates.caption: Published labeled gross anatomy of the lungs illustration. The source figure supplies no separate prose caption; original embedded labels are retained.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Left Kidney
organReferencePlates.caption: Published labeled left kidney illustration. The source figure supplies no separate prose caption; original embedded labels are retained.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Stomach
organReferencePlates.caption: The stomach has four major regions: the cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus. The addition of an inner oblique smooth muscle layer gives the muscularis the ability to vigorously churn and mix food.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Microscopic Anatomy of the Liver
organReferencePlates.caption: The liver receives oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich deoxygenated blood from the hepatic portal vein.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Exocrine and Endocrine Pancreas
organReferencePlates.caption: The pancreas has a head, a body, and a tail. It delivers pancreatic juice to the duodenum through the pancreatic duct.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Spleen
organReferencePlates.caption: (a) The spleen is attached to the stomach. (b) A micrograph of spleen tissue shows the germinal center. The marginal zone is the region between the red pulp and white pulp, which sequesters particulate antigens from the circulation and presents these antigens to lymphocytes in the white pulp. EM × 660. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of the University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Bladder
organReferencePlates.caption: (a) Anterior cross section of the bladder. (b) The detrusor muscle of the bladder (source: monkey tissue) LM × 448. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of the University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Structure of the Eye
organReferencePlates.caption: The sphere of the eye can be divided into anterior and posterior chambers. The wall of the eye is composed of three layers: the fibrous tunic, vascular tunic, and neural tunic. Within the neural tunic is the retina, with three layers of cells and two synaptic layers in between. The center of the retina has a small indentation known as the fovea.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: The Brain Stem
organReferencePlates.caption: The brain stem comprises three regions: the midbrain, the pons, and the medulla.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Thyroid Gland
organReferencePlates.caption: The thyroid gland is located in the neck where it wraps around the trachea. (a) Anterior view of the thyroid gland. (b) Posterior view of the thyroid gland. (c) The glandular tissue is composed primarily of thyroid follicles. The larger parafollicular cells often appear within the matrix of follicle cells. LM × 1332. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Adrenal Glands
organReferencePlates.caption: Both adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys and are composed of an outer cortex and an inner medulla, all surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. The cortex can be subdivided into additional zones, all of which produce different types of hormones. LM × 204. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Hypothalamus–Pituitary Complex
organReferencePlates.caption: The hypothalamus region lies inferior and anterior to the thalamus. It connects to the pituitary gland by the stalk-like infundibulum. The pituitary gland consists of an anterior and posterior lobe, with each lobe secreting different hormones in response to signals from the hypothalamus.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Small Intestine
organReferencePlates.caption: The three regions of the small intestine are the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Anatomy of the Testis
organReferencePlates.caption: This sagittal view shows the seminiferous tubules, the site of sperm production. Formed sperm are transferred to the epididymis, where they mature. They leave the epididymis during an ejaculation via the ductus deferens.
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

organReferencePlates.title: Ovaries, Uterine Tubes, and Uterus
organReferencePlates.caption: This anterior view shows the relationship of the ovaries, uterine tubes (oviducts), and uterus. Sperm enter through the vagina, and fertilization of an ovulated oocyte usually occurs in the distal uterine tube. From left to right, LM × 400, LM × 20. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)
organReferencePlates.license: OpenStax / Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; original captions and credits retained.

referenceDefinitions.method: Only exact names/synonyms or unique FMA IDs; no ambiguous merges. Explicitly unvetted and nonhuman/comparative examples excluded. Term definitions do not establish complete human attachment/innervation coverage.

atlasReadings.modifications: Anatomical identification, structure, function and relationship sections selected from archived plaintext. Clinical, treatment, variation and comparative-animal sections omitted. Original text is not a current clinical guideline. Parent muscle references are marked explicitly. Live Wikipedia revision dates were not reconstructed.
atlasReadings.license: Archived adaptations by Z-Anatomy authors: CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia contributors legacy CC BY-SA 3.0 notice retained.
atlasReadings.attribution: Each entry retains its original Wikipedia article URL, contributor-history URL, and credit. No Blender add-on code executed.

annotationValidation.method: Original source endpoint and assigned source mesh retained. Exclude endpoints outside the complete source-object bounds plus 5 mm. Nearest triangle distance is recorded separately; openings can be marked in their lumen. This checks position, not the anatomical correctness of a label.
excluded: Uncinate process of first thoracic vertebra
